To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there was no association between weight and health-related quality of live as measured by CHU-9d in children aged 5-10 years in the United Kingdom.
there is no association between weight and preference-based health related quality of life in children between the age of five and ten years old.
There was no association between weight and health-related quality of age between the ages of five and ten years.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of weight status on health utility during the early stages of life.
the relationship between weight status and health-related quality of living (HRQL) during middle childhood (6–10 years).
the relationship between weight status and health utility during childhood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there was no evidence to show that weight status impacted upon preference-based HRQL in the 6-10 year age group.
the evidence base does not currently support the use of preference-based measures for the economic evaluation of childhood weight interventions.
weight status is unlikely to be associated with preference-based HRQL in the UK population of children aged 5-10 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the association between preference-based HRQoL and weight status in young children is not consistent and that the use of such measures to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of childhood obesity interventions may be problematic.
the relationship between weight status and health utility during middle years of childhood is not as strong as it is in older children and adults.
the CHU-09D may not be a suitable instrument for use in children aged 5 to 10 in the UK.
The main takeaway from our work is that
preference-based measures may be insensitive to changes in HRQL in children, and that this may have implications for the use of such measures in economic evaluations.
the relationship between weight status and quality of life is complex and that it may change as children develop.
the CHU-10D does not appear to be a useful instrument to capture the impact of obesity on health utility in this age group.
